## ABSTRACT

When foraging in dynamic and uncertain environments, animals can benefit from basing their decisions on smart inferences about hidden properties of the world. Typical theoretical approaches to understand the strategies that animals use in such settings combine Bayesian inference and value iteration to derive optimal behavioral policies that maximize total reward given changing beliefs about the environment. However, specifying these beliefs requires infinite numerical precision; with limited resources, this problem can no longer be separated into optimizing inference and optimizing action selections. To understand the space of behavioral policies in this constrained setting, we enumerate and evaluate all possible behavioral programs that can be constructed from just a handful of states. We show that only a small fraction of the top-performing programs can be constructed by approximating Bayesian inference; the remaining programs are structurally or even functionally distinct from Bayesian. To assess structural and functional relationships among all programs, we developed novel tree embedding algorithms; these embeddings, which are capable of extracting different relational structures within the program space, reveal that nearly all good programs are closely connected through single algorithmic “mutations”. We demonstrate how one can use such relational structures to efficiently search for good solutions via an evolutionary algorithm. Moreover, these embeddings reveal that the diversity of non-Bayesian behaviors originates from a handful of key mutations that broaden the functional repertoire within the space of good programs. The fact that this diversity of behaviors does not significantly compromise performance suggests a novel approach for studying how these strategies generalize across tasks.

# An Investigation of Unsupervised Cell Tracking and Interactive Fine-Tuning
URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2025W/BIC/papers/Lalit_An_Investigation_of_Unsupervised_Cell_Tracking_and_Interactive_Fine-Tuning_ICCVW_2025_paper.pdf
Author: Manan Lalit; Jan Funke

## An Investigation of Unsupervised Cell Tracking and Interactive Fine-Tuning

#### Manan Lalit Jan Funke HHMI Janelia Research Campus 19700 Helix Drive, Ashburn, VA, USA lalitm@janelia.hhmi.org funkej@janelia.hhmi.org

### Abstract

Most existing deep learning-based cell tracking methods rely on supervised learning, requiring large-scale annotated datasets that are often unavailable in real-world scenar ios. Moreover, many approaches lack tools and methods for correcting mispredicted links or incorporating correc tions through fine-tuning. These limitations contribute to the limited adoption of deep learning-based tracking meth ods in the life sciences, where manual tracking remains the predominant approach. To reduce the annotation bur den and enable model training without extensive labeled data, we introduce a loss function for unsupervised training. Our method leverages the predictable dynamics inherent in many biological processes, providing an initialization that does not require an annotated dataset. We further in vestigate how minimal user-provided annotations can re fine tracking accuracy. To this end, we propose an active learning framework that selectively identifies uncertain de cisions within the tracking graph, allowing for efficient an notation of the most informative data points. We evaluate our approach on two microscopy datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of both our unsupervised training strat egy and active learning scheme in improving tracking per formance. Our implementation and reproducible experi ments are available at github.com/ funkelab/ attrackt and github.com/funkelab/attrackt_experiments, respectively.

### 1. Introduction

Despite decades of algorithmic development and recent ad vances in deep learning, cell tracking remains a largely manual process. A common refrain in the lab is that bi ologists prefer to manually link cell detections using tools like Mastodon [18], bypassing the automated solutions bun dled with these platforms—because correcting automated errors often takes as long as doing the task from scratch. We argue that the limited adoption of automated cell tracking methods stems from three key barriers: (i) the high cost of ac quiring ground-truth annotations for training models, (ii) the absence of decision-ranking strategies that prioritize only the most uncertain or ambiguous associations for user valida tion, omitting the trivial ones, and (iii) the lack of interactive, human-in-the-loop tools for correcting errors and refining model behavior. With a solution addressing these three chal lenges, we would be able to quantitatively analyse many developing animals at scale, thereby unlocking the potential of cell tracking to reveal the histories of cells and their roles in the complex development of animals. To address challenge (i), we introduce a unsupervised loss function, which we call Attrackt, that enables training without manual annotations. For challenge (ii), we design a heuristic active learning scheme that identifies uncertain deci sions for user annotation. Finally, to address challenge (iii), we investigate a fine-tuning strategy based on a low-rank adaptation method, allowing model refinement without over fitting on sparse labels. Our unsupervised loss Attrackt leverages the observation that many biological time-lapse datasets exhibit predictable, structured dynamics—that is, the evolution of a cell’s ap pearance over time often follows an underlying, albeit un known, process. For example, mitotic cells progress through a cyclic sequence of stages—prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase—each with characteristic morphology and visual cues. Knowing a cell’s current state provides strong predic tive power for its future appearance. These inherent temporal regularities enable Attrackt to learn meaningful associations across frames, even in the absence of manual annotations. Our unsupervised loss formulation is compatible with any tracking method that produces an association matrix—a ma trix of pairwise soft links between detections across time points. In this work, we apply Attrackt to the Trackastra [5] model, a state-of-the-art transformer-based cell tracker. By replacing Trackastra’s supervised training objective with our unsupervised loss, we enable unsupervised pre-training of its network weights. A natural question that arises post-unsupervised training is: how to query a small number of user-provided annotations (i.e., challenge (ii)) which can later be used be used to fine tune the model? To maximize tracking performance with minimal manual effort, we propose an active learning scheme that identifies a subset of uncertain decisions, which can be annotated by the user.

Once a sparse set of informative user-provided decisions is identified, one wonders how much the model benefits from these (i.e., challenge (iii)). One challenge that exists with fine-tuning on a sparse set of annotations is to not deviate too far from the original pre-trained model weights and to avoid overfitting to the limited data. To mitigate this risk of over-fitting, we explore several strategies including low-rank adaptation, which allows us to adapt only a small number of parameters in the model while keeping the rest fixed, early stopping of training, and including pseudo ground truth targets to expand the available supervision.

We show that our proposed framework—unsupervised pre-training with Attrackt, active learning-based annotation, and interactive fine-tuning—significantly improves track ing performance over using unsupervised pre-training alone. Compared to randomly sampling decisions for annotation, our selection strategy yields faster improvement, and is on par with an optimal sampling strategy. Finally, compared to training from scratch, our pre-training followed by fine tuning improves sample efficiency.

### 2. Related Work

Our approach builds upon and integrates prior research across four main themes: (i) supervised deep learning for multi-object tracking in microscopy, (ii) unsupervised deep learning for multi-object tracking, (iii) uncertainty estima tion in cell tracking, and (iv) active learning for multi-object tracking. We review each of these below.

##### 2.1. Supervised Deep Learning for Multi-Object Tracking in Microscopy

Recent years have seen a growing interest in applying deep learning to the problem of cell tracking. EmbedTrack [10], Elephant [16], and Linajea [11] learn a supervised move ment vector between consecutive frames. Elephant provides an interactive, human-in-the-loop framework for fine-tuning the model based on user supervision. Linajea provides a globally constrained optimization approach to reconstructing lineages from nuclei detections and predicted movement vec tors.
